description: ADR-0025. A rule that declares alternative ATT&CK techniques establishes none of the alternatives by default. Each decision below records, for one source rule that was read, exactly the techniques every match of it establishes, and why. A decision can only name techniques the rule declares; an empty list says the rule's logic cannot establish its technique (its detections are still shown, as declared only).

decisions.rule_name: Potential LSASS Process Dump Via Procdump
decisions.reason: Every branch requires the full-memory-dump flag and a target beginning 'ls' on the command line: that is a dump of LSASS memory whatever the binary is called. Nothing in the rule tests that the binary was renamed, so Masquerading is not established by a match.

decisions.rule_name: Potential Credential Access via LSASS Memory Dump
decisions.reason: The rule matches a process-access event whose target is lsass.exe with a memory-dump library in the call trace: an LSASS memory dump. Native API names the mechanism the author had in mind; the match does not separately establish it.
The rule matches a script host started with a .vbs script: Visual Basic execution. What the script then discovers is not observed by the rule, so Group Policy Discovery is not established by a match.

decisions.rule_name: Registry Tampering by Potentially Suspicious Processes
decisions.reason: Every branch matches a registry value being set: Modify Registry. The setting process differs by branch (several script hosts and utilities), so Visual Basic is not established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Hidden Executable In NTFS Alternate Data Stream
decisions.reason: The rule matches any stream-creation event whose file hash has an import hash, i.e. whenever a stream is created on an executable. It does not test that the stream is a named alternate data stream. Inspected on a lab recording: it fired on a browser saving a downloaded executable (the event names the file, no alternate stream, no stream contents). That event matters - it is the download of the payload - but it does not show an executable hidden in an alternate data stream.

decisions.rule_name: Potential PowerShell HackTool Script by Function Names
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Which of the many listed offensive functions is present differs by match, so none of the other declared techniques is established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter via Windows Scripts
decisions.reason: Every match is a command interpreter (PowerShell or cmd) started by a script host (wscript or mshta). Which interpreter, which script language and whether mshta was the parent differ by match, so no single sub-technique is established.
Every match is a powershell.exe process start. The obfuscation, download and decoding patterns are alternatives on the command line, so none of them is established by every match.

Every match is a command shell started directly by the service control manager: a command run through a service. Which shell differs by match; that a service was created or modified is not observed by this rule.
The rule matches a file being written whose name is that of a credential-dumping tool or its output. A file name does not show which credential store, if any, was dumped.

decisions.rule_name: Potential Antimalware Scan Interface Bypass via PowerShell
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The rule looks for strings associated with AMSI tampering; several of them also occur in code that only inspects AMSI, so tampering and obfuscation are not established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Suspicious Service was Installed in the System
decisions.reason: Every branch is a service-installation event (Security 4697 or System 7045) with a suspicious service binary: a Windows service was created. That the service then ran a command is not observed by this rule.

decisions.rule_name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Clipboard Retrieval Capabilities
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Every branch requires a call that reads the clipboard, so Clipboard Data is established as well.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Every branch requires keystroke-capture calls (key-state polling, or a keyboard hook with window tracking). Native API names the mechanism and is not separately established.
Every branch is an archiving utility adding files to an archive with a password option: Archive via Utility. Where the archived data came from is not observed.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The matched strings define types for calling native functions; that a native function was then called is not observed.
The rule matches the tool's file name alone. Neither what was dumped nor a renamed binary is observed.
The rule matches a rundll32 command line with no arguments. That is a known sign of a sacrificial process but shows none of the three declared techniques by itself.

Read from the logic, every branch is a registry value of Microsoft Defender being set to a disabling value, which looked like both declared techniques at once. The matched event in a lab recording showed otherwise: the process setting the value was Defender's own engine. The rule does not tell an adversary changing these values from the product managing its own settings, so neither technique is established by every match. (First recorded as establishing both; corrected after the event was inspected.)

Every branch is a command line containing a base64-decoding call (plain or in an encoded command): decoding at run time. The rule does not test which program was started, so PowerShell is not established by the rule itself.

decisions.rule_name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Screenshot Capabilities
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The rule requires a screen-copy call together with a bitmap type, so Screen Capture is established as well.

decisions.rule_name: Remote LSASS Process Access Through Windows Remote Management
decisions.reason: Every match is the WinRM provider host process opening LSASS: Windows Remote Management is in use. Opening the process is not a memory dump, and the PowerShell session is implied, not observed.
Every match is the WinRM provider host process, as the image or the parent: a remote-management session. PowerShell is the usual plug-in but the rule does not observe it.

decisions.rule_name: Mounting Hidden or WebDav Remote Shares
decisions.reason: Read in full: net.exe or net1.exe with 'use' and a target that is a hidden share, a WebDAV share over SSL, or an http location, excluding deletions. The three kinds of target are alternatives, and the translated branches keep the hidden-share and WebDAV patterns together, so a match does not say which was mounted. Mounting a WebDAV location is not SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and nothing in the rule observes which account was used or any account discovery. Inspected events (47, one recording): every one mounted an administrative share of another host with supplied credentials - those events are SMB/Windows Admin Shares, but the rule cannot establish that for every match. That technique is established there by another rule; nothing is lost in that recording. A decision conditioned on the matched event would recover it in general and is not supported yet.

Read in full: a child of the service control manager that either echoes a value into a named pipe or runs rundll32 on a DLL with the ',a /p:' arguments - the two published named-pipe impersonation methods of the getsystem command. Both are Token Impersonation/Theft; neither branch observes a new process being created with the token. Inspected events (two recordings): the second branch exactly, a temporary DLL run by rundll32 under services.exe.

decisions.rule_name: Deceptively named download run by the user (platform rule, ADR-0026)
decisions.reason: Written here, so its logic is known in full. A match requires two linked events on one host: a web browser saving a file, and that same file starting as a process within a day; and the file's name must end in a document, image, archive or media extension followed by .exe. The name is the double extension; the start of a browser-saved file is the user running a delivered file. Both hold for every match. It does not establish that the file is malicious.

Low-level (enrich) rule: the system-information utility starting, by image name or original file name. Every match is System Information Discovery. It is low-level because administrators run it routinely, so it never forms a cluster; it counts only once its process is linked into an existing cluster - in the inspected recordings, started by a shell that the delivered implant started.

decisions.rule_name: PowerShell Script with Token Impersonation Capabilities
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The branches are alternatives - named-pipe or thread impersonation, parent-process spoofing, token duplication, or enabling SeDebugPrivilege - and the last only enables a privilege on the script's own token. Inspected matches (APT3 CALDERA emulation): fragments of a reflective loader enabling its own debug privilege, and one token-stealing function. Access Token Manipulation is therefore not established by every match; Native API names the mechanism.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The rule requires an assembly-load call and, anywhere in the block, a byte or stream source. Assembly.Load also loads an assembly by name, so loading code from memory (Reflective Code Loading) is not established by every match, though the inspected match (APT29 day 2) was exactly that. Injection and deobfuscation are not observed.

decisions.rule_name: Suspicious Portable Executable Encoded in Powershell Script
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Every match contains 'TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA', the base64 encoding of an executable's header: an executable carried encoded inside the script (Encrypted/Encoded File). Inspected matches (APT3 CALDERA): the encoded executables embedded in a credential-dumping module and a reflective loader. Whether it was injected is not observed.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. One branch is only the name of a share-finding function. The inspected match (APT29 day 2) was that name in the alias list of an offensive module being loaded - defining the function, not enumerating shares - so Network Share Discovery is not established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Potential WinAPI Calls Via PowerShell Scripts
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Each branch is a set of native function names appearing together (injection, token or memory functions). Inspected matches (APT3 CALDERA) were fragments of a reflective loader's definitions; that a function was called, or code loaded, is not observed (as for PSReflect).

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Every branch requires creating an Outlook or Exchange Web Services object together with a mailbox or folder call: Email Collection. Which (local Outlook or remote Exchange) differs by branch, so no sub-technique. Inspected matches (APT29 day 2): an inbox-reading function from the emulation's email collection step.

The rule matches code that builds a symmetric cipher with an encryptor or decryptor. That is a capability, and none of the declared techniques follows from it: the inspected matches (APT29 day 2) were the implant's own command-channel encryption functions, which is neither an obfuscated file, decoding of a file, nor data encrypted for impact.

decisions.rule_name: Potential WMI Lateral Movement WmiPrvSE Spawned PowerShell
decisions.reason: Every match is PowerShell (by image or original file name) started by the WMI provider host: a process created through Windows Management Instrumentation. Whether it was remote (lateral movement) is not observed. Inspected matches: APT29 day 2.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The rule requires a content-writing cmdlet and the text '-stream' anywhere in the block, not together. Inspected matches (APT29 day 2) were PowerShell's own module code testing whether a drive supports streams, so writing to an alternate data stream is not established.

Read in full: certutil started with one of several verbs (download cache, decode, encode, verify, export). The verbs are alternatives, so no technique holds for every match; which one ran is on the command line.

when.reason: the URL-cache verb given a URL fetches a remote file: Ingress Tool Transfer
the decode verbs (plain or hex) turn an encoded file back into its content
exporting a certificate with its private key: Private Keys

decisions.reason: Read in full: the tool's name or any of its module prefixes on a command line; several prefixes (token, crypto, rpc, privilege) are not credential dumping, so no technique holds for every match. Which credential command ran is on the command line. A command line that only mentions a command (for example printing it) would be over-claimed; that is the same limit as every command-line decision.

when.reason: extracting credentials held by LSASS (live or from a dump of it): LSASS Memory
reading the SAM database: Security Account Manager
reading LSA secrets
reading cached domain credentials
requesting credentials by directory replication: DCSync

decisions.rule_name: Potentially Suspicious Execution From Parent Process In Public Folder
decisions.reason: Read in full: a child of a program in the Public folder that is an interpreter or a utility (bitsadmin, certutil, regsvr32, rundll32), by image or command line. Running from that folder is not hiding an artefact, so Hide Artifacts is never established; an interpreter is established when the child is one.

when.reason: the child is a command or script interpreter

decisions.rule_name: Potential Credential Access via Windows Utilities
decisions.reason: Read in full: one of several utilities that write a process memory dump (procdump, comsvcs through rundll32, and others) or ntdsutil creating a full install-from-media copy. The procdump and rundll32 branches do not test which process is dumped, so no technique holds for every match; the event shows which.

when.reason: procdump's full-memory dump given LSASS as its target (a dump file merely named after LSASS does not count): LSASS Memory
only the ntdsutil branch admits ntdsutil, and it requires a full install-from-media copy: NTDS
only the rundll32 branch admits rundll32, running a DLL export to dump: Rundll32

decisions.rule_name: Disable Security Events Logging Adding Reg Key MiniNt
decisions.reason: Every match creates the MiniNt key under the current control set (by the registry event, or by the command that adds it). With that key present Windows treats the system as Windows PE and stops writing the Security event log: Disable Windows Event Logging, done by modifying the registry. Read on the unseen recordings: the key creation event of each MiniNt procedure.

decisions.rule_name: Security Event Logging Disabled via MiniNt Registry Key - Registry Set
decisions.reason: Every match creates the MiniNt key under the current control set (by the registry event, or by the command that adds it). With that key present Windows treats the system as Windows PE and stops writing the Security event log: Disable Windows Event Logging, done by modifying the registry. This form matches the key's default value being set.

decisions.rule_name: Security Event Logging Disabled via MiniNt Registry Key - Process
decisions.reason: Every match creates the MiniNt key under the current control set (by the registry event, or by the command that adds it). With that key present Windows treats the system as Windows PE and stops writing the Security event log: Disable Windows Event Logging, done by modifying the registry. This form matches the reg.exe or PowerShell command that adds it (the limit of every command-line decision applies).

Every match is Security event 4657 - a registry value was modified - on an LSA NTLM setting: Modify Registry. The rule does not test the new value, so a weakening (Impair Defenses) is not established.

Every match sets an LSA NTLM value: Modify Registry. The RestrictSendingNTLMTraffic branch matches every value, secure ones included (the rule's own note), so a weakening is not established by every match.
Every match sets WDigest UseLogonCredential to 1: Modify Registry. That makes LSASS keep plain-text credentials for a later dump; the dump itself is not observed.
Read in full: the Rubeus tool by image, original name or description, or one of its command verbs. The tool's name alone establishes nothing; the verb on the command line says which technique ran.

when.reason: requesting service tickets to crack: Kerberoasting
injecting a ticket into the session: Pass the Ticket
extracting Kerberos tickets held in LSASS memory

decisions.reason: The rule matches a file written with the .kirbi extension. As for dropped credential-tool files, a file name shows neither which credential store was read nor whether a ticket was stolen or legitimately requested.

Every match is bitsadmin creating or running a BITS transfer job: BITS Jobs. The transfer may be an upload (/upload) as well as a download, so Ingress Tool Transfer is not established by every match; a renamed binary is not tested.
Every branch creates, configures or resumes a BITS job (bitsadmin verbs or the PowerShell BITS cmdlets): BITS Jobs. The direction of the transfer is not tested.
Read in full: a CPL registered under the Control Panel key, or a command line ending in a .cpl outside the system directory. The branches differ; the second is a control panel item being run.

when.reason: a control panel item run from its own path: Control Panel

decisions.rule_name: Command Shell Activity Started via RunDLL32
decisions.reason: Every match is cmd or PowerShell started by rundll32 with a command line: code run through rundll32 started a shell - Rundll32 proxy execution and a command interpreter. Unsecured credentials are not observed.

when.reason: the child is cmd: Windows Command Shell
the child is PowerShell

decisions.rule_name: HTML Help HH.EXE Suspicious Child Process
decisions.reason: Every match is one of a list of interpreters and utilities started by hh.exe: content of a compiled HTML file ran a program - Compiled HTML File proxy execution. Which child differs by match; phishing delivery is not observed.

when.reason: the child is cmd: Windows Command Shell
the child is PowerShell

decisions.rule_name: Process Activity via Compiled HTML File
decisions.reason: Every match is a script host, shell or mshta started by hh.exe: Compiled HTML File proxy execution. Which child differs by match; that a user opened a delivered file is not observed.

when.reason: the child is cmd: Windows Command Shell
the child is PowerShell

decisions.reason: Low-level rule: hh.exe opening a .chm file - compiled HTML content being run. Low-level because users open help files routinely; it counts only once linked into a cluster (Amendment I).

Low-level rule with alternative branches: user-session utilities (whoami, quser, qwinsta), or local account listing (net user, wmic useraccount, cmd dir of the profiles directory, cmdkey /l). Each branch's program says which; counted only once linked into a cluster (Amendment I).

when.reason: the program reports the current or logged-on users: System Owner/User Discovery
the net user and wmic useraccount branches list local accounts: Local Account

decisions.reason: Read in full: alternative discovery commands (nbtstat, arp, nltest, nslookup for domain controllers, dsquery subnet, net group /domain). The program says which.

when.reason: only the net group /domain branch admits net: Domain Groups
nltest listing or locating domain controllers: Remote System Discovery

decisions.reason: Every match is the System process (the SMB server) writing iertutil.dll into the Internet Explorer directory: a file placed in a system directory over an administrative share. The DCOM execution that would follow is not observed.

decisions.rule_name: DCOM InternetExplorer.Application Iertutil DLL Hijack - Security
decisions.reason: Every match is Security event 5145 (a network share object was accessed) for iertutil.dll in the Internet Explorer directory by a user account: SMB/Windows Admin Shares. The DCOM execution is not observed.

decisions.rule_name: Potential DCOM InternetExplorer.Application DLL Hijack - Image Load
decisions.reason: The rule matches iexplore loading iertutil.dll from its own directory: a planted DLL being loaded (DLL hijacking, not declared). Neither SMB shares nor DCOM are observed by this event.

Every match is System event 7045 - a service was installed - with a command or admin-share binary as its image: a Windows service was created. That it ran, or how the binary arrived, differs by branch.
Every match writes a service's configuration under the Services key with a command or admin-share binary: a Windows service was created or modified. That it ran is not observed.
Every match is Security event 4697 - a service was installed - with a command or admin-share binary: a Windows service was created. That it ran is not observed.

decisions.rule_name: Microsoft Exchange Worker Spawning Suspicious Processes
decisions.reason: Every match is a shell started by an Exchange application-pool worker: code running inside Exchange's web server started a command interpreter. Whether through a web shell or an exploited flaw differs, so neither is established.

when.reason: the child is cmd: Windows Command Shell
the child is PowerShell

left_ambiguous_after_reading.why: Matches the PsExec client by name; PsExec also runs commands locally.

left_ambiguous_after_reading.rule_name: Potential Arbitrary Command Execution Via FTP.EXE
left_ambiguous_after_reading.why: One branch is a child of ftp.exe, the other only an ftp script option.
A memory dump through comsvcs.dll; the rule does not test which process is dumped.

Alternative credential techniques by branch (LSASS, SAM, secrets, DCSync, vaults, DPAPI, pass-the-hash, tickets, certificates); inspected matches include the module's own help text. PowerShell is not declared.
